title: Fragment of a different recording on Louisiana musicians
summary: An unidentified voice and questioner discuss clarinet systems, Joe Rivette, Freddie Neumann's band at the Silver Slipper and an earlier interview.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: New Orleans and Louisiana, everybody, if you'd like to tell you anything about many other bands.

Maybe we can do another reel, huh? And talk about Mississippi musicians. Of course, I want to talk about a lot of people. Like where Bert Sigerson is now. To find him, you reminded me of that. What Sidney Ayrton used to call a BAME system clarinet, what he called an ALBA system. Yeah. What did you say it was?

Well, Sidney referred to the ALBA system clarinet as a few key. He referred to the BAME system clarinet, which had so many more keys, as a thousand-legged clarinet. And, of course, Sidney was extremely interesting to me. And he played in South Louisiana with a little dance down there for years. He played with Joe Rivette. And Joe Rivette was very famous to that part of Louisiana in the 30s. Sidney, well, they used to have a little slogan, it's a swingin' sweat with Joe Rivette. He later became a gambler, a professional gambler, was in Las Vegas for a long period of years. But he was a good guitarist. Well, who was the leader of that band? It was Freddie Newman's band. Freddie Newman's band. Freddie Newman's band. Freddie had stayed on, Sharky and Monk Hazel. Yeah. And Nina had quit, but Monk Hazel, there wasn't anything else to do. So they wanted to work, and so they had stayed on at this little Silver Slipper. It was just below 327. It must have been in the 400 block of Burbank. It may have been in the 300 block, I can't be sure.

I swear I heard... Excuse me, go ahead. That's where I interviewed Jack and where I interviewed Noxy. No kidding. Yeah. You know, and eventually the name of it changed. And it eventually became one of these banjo places your father's playing.
